source.title: From Data to Knowledge: Evaluating How Efficiently Language Models Learn Facts
source.authors: D. Christoph; Max Ploner; Patrick Haller; Alan Akbik

record.tranche_reason: The study compares factual-probe and evaluation-task performance across model sizes, bearing on downstream performance versus scale, but it does not measure the original held-out-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study does not test held-out pretraining cross-entropy, predict losses from smaller runs, or examine compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. It does measure downstream factual accuracy across model sizes, so the rows below bear on V6. The fact-frequency probability curve and its fitted α values concern factual recall versus estimated fact exposure, not the loss-scaling versions.
record.test_reason: The study's own factual-recall and downstream-task accuracies at two sizes per architecture bear on V6 in a controlled Wikipedia-pretraining setting. They test local size trends, but do not establish a predictive scaling function. The fitted fact-frequency curve does not test pretraining-loss scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that larger tested models learn low-frequency facts more efficiently, while high-frequency performance has less size separation and no consistent size ordering. LLAMA leads their sample-efficiency measures, followed by MAMBA 2. They also emphasize metric agreement and robustness to evaluation fact-frequency composition. Whether the size trend extends beyond one billion parameters remains open.
record.recipe_differences: This study measures factual recall and estimates fact exposure from corpus co-occurrence; it does not reproduce cross-entropy scaling sweeps, loss extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance patterns vary with fact-frequency split, model architecture, evaluation dataset, and metric.

fits_no_version.finding: The study fits a power-shaped relationship between factual recall probability and estimated entity-pair frequency, with model-specific α values.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Factual recall probability increases with estimated fact exposure according to a fitted power-shaped saturation curve.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed α metric varies less than raw accuracy under changes in the evaluation set's fact-frequency composition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Exposure-adjusted sample-efficiency metrics can be more robust to evaluation frequency composition than raw accuracy.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the First Workshop on Large Language Model Memorization (L2M2)
record.problems: Only small-to-medium models are tested, with two sizes per architecture. Fact counts use a simple entity co-occurrence heuristic that can miss occurrences or misidentify relations; the paper notes that fact-frequency splits and sparse buckets can affect metric reliability.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the BEAR-big high/low-frequency split results in Appendix Table 6 and the language-model evaluation-harness perplexity values in Appendix Table 7 to remain within the 60-row limit; the retained rows cover the main BEAR size/frequency comparisons and task-accuracy measures.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss following power laws across several orders of magnitude.
Predicting losses of substantially larger runs from small-run fits.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its stability across compute budgets.
Architecture effects on loss at fixed parameter count across a wide range of shapes.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
A fitted or validated quantitative prediction of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss; extrapolation beyond two small-to-medium sizes per architecture.
Setup or fitting dependence of pretraining-loss scaling exponents and compute-optimal allocation.

missing.what: Downstream factual accuracy versus training progress: Figures 12 and 15 show BEAR and BEAR-big accuracy trajectories across 42 checkpoints for all eight models. Section 4.2 reports early stabilization of frequency-conditioned accuracy and smaller later changes. These provide the token-scale dimension missing from the endpoint rows, without establishing a quantitative prediction law.

record.verdict_notes: All retained numbers match the supplied tables. The 56 rows represent 28 comparisons twice; endpoint direction should not change a comparison's state. Reported endpoint errors do not establish significance of paired differences, and overlapping errors alone do not prove absence. Table 2's threshold is 1024, despite prose using 1000. BEAR-big frequency splits and evaluation perplexities are explicitly declared omitted, so they are not missing-row entries. No original-source exclusion applies.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Predicting much larger runs' loss from smaller runs.
Architecture effects on held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
The study compares performance at two model sizes; it does not fit or evaluate a predictive relationship with pretraining loss, nor extrapolate to larger sizes.
Dependence of loss-scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Overall BEAR and BEAR-big accuracy, and low-frequency BEAR facts, within each architecture
relationships.reason: Larger models improve in every architecture: BEAR gains 2.4–3.5 points, low-frequency gains 2.4–3.7, and BEAR-big gains 1.5–2.4 (r2, r4, r6, r8, r10, r12, r14, r16, r26, r28, r30, r32).
relationships.display_finding: Larger models gained 2.4–3.5 accuracy points on BEAR, 2.4–3.7 on low-frequency facts and 1.5–2.4 on BEAR-big across architectures.

relationships.condition: High-frequency BEAR facts for GPT2 and XLSTM
relationships.reason: Accuracy increases from 83.4% to 87.5% for GPT2 and 79.4% to 82.2% for XLSTM (r18, r22).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased from 83.4% to 87.5% for GPT2 and from 79.4% to 82.2% for XLSTM.

relationships.condition: High-frequency BEAR facts for LLAMA and MAMBA 2; point estimates only
relationships.reason: Increasing size lowers accuracy from 88.7% to 85.4% and 82.2% to 81.4%, respectively; uncertainty is unreported (r20, r24), and the authors explicitly report no consistent size trend.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy fell from 88.7% to 85.4% for LLAMA and 82.2% to 81.4% for MAMBA 2, without reported uncertainty or a consistent overall size trend.

relationships.reason: Accuracy increases from 9.35% ±0.41% to 11.97% ±0.45% with size (r54).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased with size from 9.35% ±0.41% to 11.97% ±0.45%.

relationships.condition: Winogrande across all architectures; WSC273 for GPT2 and MAMBA 2; LAMBADA for LLAMA and MAMBA 2
relationships.reason: Size gains are small or uncertain relative to reported errors, giving incomplete evidence for predictable improvement (r34, r36, r38, r40, r42, r48, r52, r56).
relationships.display_finding: Size gains were small or uncertain relative to reported errors across the specified architecture and task combinations.

relationships.condition: WSC273 for LLAMA and XLSTM; LAMBADA for GPT2
relationships.reason: Point estimates decline with size, but reported errors and the absence of paired significance tests prevent a firm reversal conclusion (r44, r46, r50).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy estimates declined with size, but reported errors and absent paired significance tests left the reversals uncertain.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: BEAR and BEAR-big overall accuracy; low-frequency BEAR facts; Winogrande and several WSC273/LAMBADA model comparisons
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy is higher for the medium model in each architecture on the overall BEAR and BEAR-big results and on all four architectures' low-frequency BEAR facts; several evaluation-task comparisons also increase with size (r2, r4, r6, r8, r10, r12, r14, r16, r26, r28, r30, r32, r34, r36, r38, r40, r42, r48, r52, r54, r56).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: High-frequency BEAR facts and WSC273/LAMBADA task comparisons
reader_labels.reason: The size trend is not uniform: larger models score lower on high-frequency facts for LLAMA and MAMBA 2, and several WSC273 and LAMBADA comparisons favor smaller models or show only small changes (r19, r20, r23, r24, r43, r44, r45, r46, r49, r50, r51, r53, r55).
